paragraphs: Distributed optimization divides a learning problem across multiple computing nodes. The difficulty is not just doing the calculations: nodes also need to exchange information to coordinate their updates. This paper develops a stochastic version of the alternating direction method of multipliers, or ADMM, that reduces how frequently that communication must happen.

The proposed method supports multiple blocks of variables and runs their updates fully in parallel. Each node only needs to perform simple stochastic gradient descent updates. The method also accommodates arbitrary block structures, making its organization flexible rather than tied to one particular partition of the optimization variables.

The central result concerns the relationship between computation and communication. Whereas the existing ADMM methods discussed in the abstract communicate roughly once per computation round, the proposed method requires communication rounds proportional to the square root of the computation rounds. Its convergence rate remains comparable to or better than existing stochastic ADMM methods. Together, these claims show that reducing coordination frequency need not sacrifice the stated optimization guarantees.
neurips-2019-a-communication-efficient-s.tldr: A parallel stochastic ADMM method reduces communication rounds to the square root of computation rounds while retaining competitive convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Training an image model to withstand one kind of corruption can make it less reliable on another. This paper examines that tradeoff through the frequency content of image changes. High frequencies describe rapidly varying image patterns, while low frequencies describe more slowly varying structure. This perspective helps organize robustness gains and losses that otherwise appear to be separate effects.

The authors study Gaussian data augmentation and adversarial training. They find that both improve robustness to corruptions concentrated at high frequencies while reducing robustness to corruptions concentrated at low frequencies. The result identifies a shared pattern across these two training approaches, rather than treating robustness as a single property that improves uniformly.

These observations suggest that a more diverse collection of augmentations could help mitigate the tradeoff. The authors also report that AutoAugment achieves state-of-the-art robustness on CIFAR-10-C despite being optimized for accuracy on clean images. That finding supports the value of augmentation diversity, while the frequency analysis explains why gains against one family of corruptions need not extend to others.
neurips-2019-a-fourier-perspective-on-mo.tldr: Frequency analysis reveals why Gaussian augmentation and adversarial training can improve robustness to some image corruptions while worsening it for others.

paragraphs: Deep neural networks and Gaussian processes offer different ways to learn relationships from data. Although theoretical connections between them were already known, this paper focuses on how their training procedures relate. Its starting point is Bayesian neural networks, where learning involves a distribution over model parameters rather than only a single fitted parameter setting.

The authors show that certain Gaussian approximations to a Bayesian network's posterior are equivalent to Gaussian process posteriors. This lets them interpret both solutions and intermediate iterations of a deep-learning algorithm through Gaussian process inference. The equivalence concerns those particular approximations; it does not assert that every neural network training procedure is Gaussian process inference.

One consequence is that training a network can also produce a Gaussian process kernel and a nonlinear feature map. The resulting kernel is the neural tangent kernel. The authors show examples learned from real datasets and demonstrate tuning network hyperparameters using Gaussian process marginal likelihood. The contribution therefore connects training behavior to a probabilistic framework that supplies an additional tool for choosing model settings.
neurips-2019-approximate-inference-turns.tldr: Certain Gaussian posterior approximations connect Bayesian neural network training directly to Gaussian process inference and hyperparameter tuning.

paragraphs: Column subset selection asks whether a matrix can be represented accurately using a small collection of its own columns. This paper measures reconstruction error by adding the absolute errors of individual entries. In the worst case, obtaining an approximation within a factor of 1 + epsilon can require a number of columns that grows substantially with matrix size.

The authors obtain a much more favorable result under a distributional assumption. The input must be an arbitrary rank-k matrix plus noise whose entries are independent and identically distributed. If the noise has a finite moment of order 1 + gamma for any fixed positive gamma, their method achieves the desired approximation in nearly linear time, using poly(k/epsilon) + O(k log n) columns.

A complementary impossibility result shows why noise assumptions matter: without a finite first moment, even allowing n^{o(1)} columns cannot provide the stated approximation guarantee. The findings establish a tractable setting despite the difficult worst case. They do not settle every distribution between the sufficient higher-moment condition and the failure of the first moment.
neurips-2019-average-case-column-subset-.tldr: Under a mild finite-moment noise assumption, column subset selection achieves near-optimal entrywise absolute-error approximation in nearly linear time.

paragraphs: A neural network's level set consists of inputs where its output takes a particular value. Such sets can describe a classifier's decision boundary or represent a curve or surface. This paper develops a way to control that geometry directly during learning, making the positions of points on a level set part of the training objective.

The method first samples points from the network's level sets. It then relates the positions of those points to the network parameters through a sample network, constructed by adding one fixed linear layer to the original network. This connection allows a loss function to act on the sampled geometry and influence how the underlying network changes.

The authors test the approach on generalization, adversarial robustness, and reconstruction of curves and surfaces from point clouds. They report high-fidelity surfaces reconstructed directly from raw three-dimensional point clouds. For small to medium networks, they also obtain adversarially robust accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art methods. These findings show how one mechanism for controlling level sets can serve several distinct learning objectives.
neurips-2019-controlling-neural-level-se.tldr: Sampling neural level sets and linking their positions to network parameters enables direct training of decision-boundary and surface geometry.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups objects using pairwise judgments of whether they are similar or dissimilar. A disagreement occurs when a clustering separates a similar pair or places a dissimilar pair together. The usual objective is to minimize these disagreements. This paper adds a second concern: obtaining the pairwise judgments can itself be costly.

The authors treat similarity information as something an algorithm must actively request. Instead of assuming that every pairwise score is already available, their algorithms choose queries while constructing a clustering. The goal is therefore to balance the quality of the resulting groups against the amount of information collected.

The paper provides simple active learning algorithms with provable, almost optimal tradeoffs and guarantees concerning cluster recovery, alongside tests on different datasets. It also establishes information-theoretic lower bounds on the queries needed to guarantee a chosen disagreement level. These two sides clarify both what the algorithms can achieve and how much querying is fundamentally necessary. The contribution is a characterization of the cost of information in clustering, not merely a procedure that asks fewer questions.
neurips-2019-correlation-clustering-with.tldr: Adaptive similarity queries yield provably near-optimal tradeoffs between clustering disagreements and the cost of collecting pairwise information.

paragraphs: An NMR spectrum contains information about a molecule's bond structure, but interpreting that information can require substantial human effort. This paper tackles the inverse problem of recovering chemical structure from a molecular formula and spectrum. It represents the task as predicting a graph: atoms are vertices, and bonds are edges with types.

The method builds a molecule incrementally, choosing one bond at a time within a Markov decision process. A deep neural network learns these choices through imitation learning. During training, it imitates an oracle that knows which remaining bonds are correct. The approach also uses information attached to some vertices and generates graphs subject to vertex constraints.

The authors report quickly recovering the correct structure for a wide variety of molecules and recognizing with reasonable certainty when the method cannot do so. They describe the use of vertex information and constraints as a first among recent chemical graph generation approaches. The results point toward automated structure identification; active learning for spectroscopy is presented as a potential further direction.
neurips-2019-deep-imitation-learning-for.tldr: A neural network trained to imitate correct bond choices reconstructs molecular graphs from formulas and NMR spectra.

paragraphs: Combining calculations from distributed machines becomes tricky when matrix inversion is involved. Inverting locally and then averaging does not generally give the same result as combining the matrices before inversion. This creates inversion bias in distributed Newton optimization, where local machines estimate an update using an inverse Hessian and a gradient.

The paper proposes determinantal averaging to correct this bias. Each locally estimated Newton step receives a weight proportional to the determinant of its local Hessian estimate. The weighted estimates are then combined. This changes how local information contributes to the global result, addressing the mismatch that a uniform average leaves unresolved.

The authors prove asymptotic consistency: the resulting estimate recovers the exact Newton step as the number of distributed partitions tends to infinity. This is a limiting guarantee, rather than a claim of exact recovery with finitely many partitions. Their proof develops identities and moment bounds for random-matrix determinants and adjugates. The method also applies to linear transformations of matrix inverses, including the trace of an inverse covariance matrix used in uncertainty quantification.
neurips-2019-distributed-estimation-of-t.tldr: Weighting local Newton estimates by Hessian determinants corrects inversion bias and recovers the exact step as distributed partitions grow without bound.

paragraphs: Artificial agents can develop communication protocols when cooperation requires them to exchange information. Those protocols sometimes display language-like structure, including compositionality: the organization of messages from meaningful parts. This paper asks how the conditions under which agents learn to communicate influence the structure that eventually emerges.

The authors introduce ease of teaching as a training pressure. They periodically replace established agents with new ones, studying replacement both sequentially and within a population. This makes the arrival of inexperienced participants part of the communication setting. The intervention examines language development when communication must accommodate new learners as well as support the cooperative task.

The paper reports that this pressure affects the structure of the resulting language. Its contribution is to connect agent replacement with properties of learned communication protocols, extending the investigation of how training environments shape emergent language. The stated finding is an effect on structure; the abstract does not characterize that effect as a universal increase in compositionality. The study therefore focuses on teachability as a factor in language formation.
neurips-2019-ease-of-teaching-and-langua.tldr: Periodically introducing new agents creates an ease-of-teaching pressure that affects the structure of emergent communication.

paragraphs: Adding noise to a statistical summary does not automatically provide differential privacy. This paper studies when noise from elliptical distributions can supply that guarantee, including settings with infinitely many dimensions. It examines both the compatibility of the resulting probability distributions and the strength of privacy that these perturbations can achieve.

A necessary condition identified in the paper is that all possible input databases induce equivalent probability measures. For elliptical distributions sharing a dispersion operator C, the authors show equivalence when the difference between their means belongs to C's Cameron-Martin space. For finite-dimensional summaries, they also reduce calculation of the privacy parameter epsilon to a one-dimensional maximization problem.

The authors apply this analysis to multivariate Laplace, t, Gaussian, and K-norm noise. One finding is that multivariate Laplace noise does not achieve pure epsilon differential privacy in dimensions above one. In infinite-dimensional spaces, no elliptical distribution can provide pure epsilon privacy; only approximate privacy may be possible. The distinction matters because the distribution family and dimension constrain which privacy guarantee a noise mechanism can support.
neurips-2019-elliptical-perturbations-fo.tldr: The paper characterizes privacy conditions for elliptical noise and proves barriers to pure differential privacy in higher and infinite dimensions.

paragraphs: Many inverse problems estimate hidden quantities by finding the minimum of an energy function. The function assigns a cost to candidate solutions, so changing its weights can change which solution is preferred. This paper asks how to learn those weights when the quantity of interest is the location of the resulting minimum.

The proposed technique, Wibergian Learning, formally links energy-function parameters to minima by representing minima as fixed points of optimization methods. A fixed point is a state that an optimization update leaves unchanged. This formulation gives a way to describe how an estimated solution depends on the weights that shape the energy.

That dependency enables gradient-based training across the combined system, connecting deep learning with classical methods for inverse problems. Rather than learning an energy independently of how its minimum is used, the approach supports end-to-end optimization. The authors demonstrate applications to tracker fusion and multiview three-dimensional reconstruction, reporting state-of-the-art results in both. These examples show the relevance of learning through the optimization solution across distinct estimation tasks.
neurips-2019-fixing-implicit-derivatives.tldr: Wibergian Learning links energy minima to trainable weights through optimization fixed points, enabling end-to-end learning for inverse problems.

paragraphs: Causal identification asks whether the distribution produced by an intervention can be computed from observational data and qualitative knowledge of causal relationships. That knowledge is often represented by a causal diagram. This paper considers the harder situation where the available information determines only a class of Markov equivalent diagrams, rather than one fully specified diagram.

Working with an equivalence class preserves uncertainty about the causal structure instead of choosing a single diagram. The paper focuses on conditional causal effects, which describe intervention outcomes conditional on additional information. These effects are particularly relevant when evaluating plans or policies whose decisions depend on observed conditions.

An earlier algorithm addressed unconditional effects given a Markov equivalence class, but some identifiable conditional effects fall outside what that algorithm can handle. The authors derive an algorithm for identifying conditional effects to address this gap. The contribution concerns what intervention quantities can be recovered despite structural ambiguity. It extends the available identification tools toward conditional policy evaluation without requiring the starting knowledge to specify one complete causal diagram.
neurips-2019-identification-of-condition.tldr: An identification algorithm addresses conditional causal effects when causal knowledge specifies only a Markov equivalence class.

paragraphs: Fair representation learning aims to preserve useful predictive information while reducing disparities associated with population groups. This paper examines whether those goals can always be achieved together. Using information theory, it quantifies a tradeoff between demographic parity and the combined predictive utility across groups.

The negative result applies when groups have different base rates, meaning different prevalences of the outcome being predicted. In that setting, the authors establish an information-theoretic lower bound on joint prediction error for methods seeking fair representations. The significance is that the tradeoff is not merely a weakness of a particular adversarial training algorithm; it reflects a constraint on what such representations can accomplish.

The paper also gives a conditional positive result. If the optimal decision functions for different groups are close, learning fair representations leads to accuracy parity, meaning similar error rates across groups. This is a different fairness criterion from demographic parity. Experiments on real-world datasets support the theoretical findings, highlighting both the costs of pursuing one fairness objective and conditions under which another can emerge.
neurips-2019-inherent-tradeoffs-in-learn.tldr: Information-theoretic bounds expose fairness–accuracy tradeoffs when group base rates differ, alongside conditions supporting similar error rates across groups.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows build probabilistic generative models using invertible transformations. Training and sampling repeatedly require inverses and Jacobian determinants, so the computational cost of these operations shapes which architectures are practical. This paper investigates convolutional transformations as an alternative to architectures constrained to diagonal, triangular, or low-rank Jacobian structures.

The proposed flows use circular and symmetric convolutions. For these transforms, both determinant evaluation and inverse mapping through deconvolution can be performed in O(N log N) time. The authors also show that elementwise multiplication can be combined with these operations to increase modeling flexibility while building on the proposed transform family.

A second contribution is an analytic method for designing nonlinear, invertible elementwise transformations. These transformations can induce desired properties in intermediate layers by implicitly introducing particular regularizers into the loss. The authors show that the resulting components support more effective generative image models. The broader contribution is an expanded set of flow transformations whose inverse and determinant calculations remain efficient, allowing computational tractability and modeling flexibility to be considered together.
neurips-2019-invertible-convolutional-fl.tldr: Circular and symmetric convolutions provide flexible normalizing-flow components with efficient inverse and Jacobian determinant computations.

paragraphs: A generative adversarial network learns by reducing a measure of difference between generated and real data distributions. This paper argues that the choice of measure should reflect how the generated data will later be used for learning. In particular, the relevant prediction models and their loss function should influence what counts as a meaningful distributional difference.

The authors adopt discrepancy, a measure developed for domain adaptation that incorporates both the hypothesis set and the loss. They establish properties useful for GAN training and prove explicit generalization guarantees. This gives the training objective a connection to the structure of the downstream learning task, rather than evaluating distributional similarity without that context.

The paper develops two efficient algorithms: DGAN trains a generator directly, while EDGAN combines previously trained generative models. Experiments on toy examples and benchmark datasets find DGAN competitive with other GANs and EDGAN better than existing GAN ensembles, including AdaGAN. The contribution thus covers both learning a new generator and choosing how to combine existing ones through a task-sensitive discrepancy measure.
neurips-2019-learning-gans-and-ensembles.tldr: A discrepancy measure sensitive to downstream models and losses supports GAN training, generator ensembles, and explicit generalization guarantees.

paragraphs: Semantic image synthesis turns a layout of labeled regions into a photorealistic image. The layout specifies what belongs at each location, and the generator must turn that spatial information into image content. This paper argues that the generator's convolutional kernels should themselves depend on the semantic labels they are processing.

The proposed approach predicts convolutional kernels from the semantic label map. Those kernels transform noise maps into intermediate features and ultimately into an image. This makes the operations that construct the image responsive to the layout, extending conditioning beyond supplying labels as inputs or using them to adjust normalized activations.

The authors also introduce a discriminator that embeds semantic information in a feature pyramid. They report that it improves fine detail and alignment between generated images and input layouts compared with previous multi-scale discriminators. Across several semantic segmentation datasets, the overall approach achieves state-of-the-art quantitative and subjective evaluation results. The findings support conditioning both image construction and image assessment more directly on the requested semantic structure.
neurips-2019-learning-to-predict-layout-.tldr: Predicting convolutional kernels from semantic layouts improves image synthesis, supported by a discriminator designed for detail and semantic alignment.

paragraphs: An exploration agent has limited time to discover an unfamiliar environment. This paper asks whether it can learn an exploration strategy from other environments and transfer that strategy to a new one. The objective is to visit as many distinct states as possible within a fixed number of steps, with training and test environments drawn from the same distribution.

The authors focus on environments whose states and transitions form a graph. They formulate exploration as reinforcement learning, rewarding the agent when it reaches a state it has not previously visited. A graph-structured memory records its past trajectory, giving the policy a representation of its exploration history.

The approach is evaluated on spatial maps and on coverage-guided testing of domain-specific programs and real-world mobile applications. The authors report strong map exploration performance and better software-testing performance than methods designed by human experts. These results support learning reusable exploration behavior across related environments. The transfer claim remains tied to unseen environments from the training distribution, rather than arbitrary environments with unrelated structure.
neurips-2019-learning-transferable-graph.tldr: A reinforcement learning policy with graph memory learns exploration strategies that transfer to unseen environments from the same distribution.

paragraphs: Multi-object tracking requires associating detections across observations so that they form consistent object tracks. One widely used formulation expresses this association problem as a minimum-cost flow problem on a graph. This paper targets the computational burden of solving those graphs, which can limit the scale of tracking problems that are practical to process.

The authors develop minimum-update Successive Shortest Path, or muSSP, by exploiting structural properties specific to tracking graphs. The approach specializes the solver to this setting rather than relying on a generic flow algorithm with only small modifications. They prove that muSSP returns an exact optimal solution to the formulated flow problem.

The evaluation includes 40 experiments across five tracking datasets, with different detection results and graph designs. muSSP is the fastest of the compared solvers in every experiment, with reported improvements of 5 to 337 times over the best competitor. These findings demonstrate substantial computational gains in the tested settings while retaining exact optimization. The optimality guarantee concerns the flow objective used for association.
neurips-2019-mussp-efficient-min-cost-fl.tldr: muSSP exploits tracking-graph structure to solve minimum-cost flow exactly, with large speedups across the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Relational inference seeks to discover how entities interact while learning the dynamics those interactions produce. This paper addresses systems with multiple interaction types by treating inference as modular meta-learning. Neural modules are learned across tasks and then composed in different ways to explain particular observed systems.

Choosing a composition becomes the inner optimization problem of the meta-learning procedure. This formulation implicitly encodes time invariance and evaluates relations in the context of other relations, increasing inference capacity. The authors describe the resulting model-based approach as more data-efficient and capable of estimating states of unobserved entities whose presence can be inferred through their effects on observed ones.

Searching possible graph neural network compositions is computationally demanding. To accelerate that search, the authors also meta-learn a proposal function for the inner-loop simulated annealing procedure. They report that this increases the size of addressable problems by two orders of magnitude. The contribution combines reusable interaction modules with a learned search mechanism, addressing both the expressiveness of relational inference and the cost of finding suitable compositions.
neurips-2019-neural-relational-inference.tldr: Modular meta-learning infers interacting systems through reusable neural components, while learned search proposals enable much larger problems.

paragraphs: Nonlinear manifold learning methods place high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space to reveal structure visually. Their objectives are nonconvex, so optimization can settle into a poor local minimum. Once there, ordinary updates may stop improving the arrangement even though the resulting embedding does not represent the data well.

This paper proposes an extension to several such methods that identifies pressured points: points caught in poor local minima with low embedding quality. It temporarily gives those points access to one additional embedding dimension. The extra freedom changes the space in which they can move, allowing the method to improve an arrangement that was stuck in the original space.

The authors show that this temporary dimensional expansion can decrease the objective function, including after an existing method has reached a poor local minimum. The contribution therefore offers a way to continue improving embeddings beyond the stopping point of the original optimization. The stated result is an improvement in objective value, rather than a guarantee that every local minimum is escaped or that a global optimum is found.
neurips-2019-no-pressure-addressing-the-.tldr: Temporarily giving poorly embedded points an extra dimension can improve manifold-learning objectives after optimization becomes stuck.

paragraphs: In a multi-armed bandit problem, a learner repeatedly chooses an action while seeing only limited reward information. Perturbation-based algorithms randomize action selection by adding noise to their estimates. This paper investigates which noise distributions can achieve optimal regret, a measure of the reward lost through the learner's decisions.

For stochastic bandits with sub-Gaussian rewards, the authors provide a unified regret analysis covering sub-Weibull and bounded perturbations. Instance-optimal bounds hold for sub-Weibull perturbations with parameter two and a matching lower-tail bound. They also hold for bounded perturbations with enough probability mass near the extremes of their support. These qualifications make the distribution's tail behavior central to the guarantee.

For adversarial bandits, the authors establish rigorous obstacles to two natural approaches, drawing on discrete choice and extreme value theory. Their findings suggest that an optimal perturbation, if one exists, would be of Frechet type. This is a proposed direction supported by the barriers, rather than a construction proving adversarial optimality. The paper thus distinguishes established stochastic guarantees from unresolved possibilities in the adversarial setting.
neurips-2019-on-the-optimality-of-pertur.tldr: Perturbation tail conditions yield optimal stochastic-bandit regret, while adversarial barriers suggest a possible role for Frechet-type noise.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimistic regret-minimization algorithms for zero-sum extensive-form games, addressing both regret reduction and Nash equilibrium computation. Applying these methods requires geometry suited to the structured space of game strategies. The authors investigate dilated entropy and Euclidean distance functions, proving explicit strong-convexity bounds for the latter on general treeplexes.

These distance functions let mirror descent and optimistic mirror descent decompose into local algorithms at each information set. That organization resembles counterfactual regret minimization and supports practical techniques such as distributed updates and pruning rarely active parts of the game tree. The proposed algorithms have a proven convergence rate of T^{-1}.

Experiments reveal an important distinction between the guarantee and practical comparisons. The optimistic methods converge faster than T^{-1} in an example matrix game where CFR+ converges at roughly T^{-0.74}, and fast convergence also appears in Kuhn poker. However, CFR+ remains faster for equilibrium computation in deeper game trees. When the objective is minimizing regret, the optimistic methods can outperform CFR+ even in those deeper games.
neurips-2019-optimistic-regret-minimizat.tldr: Dilated distance functions enable local optimistic updates with T^{-1} convergence guarantees, though practical advantages over CFR+ depend on the task and game.

paragraphs: Neural network loss surfaces are generally difficult to optimize, but their geometry can have more structure within particular regions. This paper studies feed-forward networks with ReLU activations and weight decay. It shows that the regularized loss is piecewise strongly convex on an important open set, which contains every global minimizer under additional conditions.

Within that set, the authors prove that local minima are isolated and every differentiable critical point is a local minimum. These are regional statements about the regularized objective, rather than a claim that the entire network loss is convex. For linear neural networks, they also rule out nonzero critical points satisfying a specified training-error threshold within a norm ball.

Experiments on three standard image classification problems examine the geometry encountered along stochastic gradient descent trajectories. The authors find the regularized loss almost always exhibits piecewise strong convexity along those trajectories. This empirical observation complements the theory by suggesting that the analyzed geometry appears during training, while the formal conclusions remain tied to the stated set and conditions.
neurips-2019-piecewise-strong-convexity-.tldr: Weight-decayed ReLU networks have piecewise strongly convex loss geometry on a specified region, yielding conditional guarantees about critical points.

paragraphs: Privately selecting the most frequent items becomes difficult when the universe of possible items is large or unknown. Common methods require counts for every domain element. This paper develops user-level differentially private top-k selection algorithms that need access only to the actual top-k-prime items, where k-prime can be any chosen value at least as large as k.

The algorithms provide approximate differential privacy without requiring knowledge of the full domain. The authors consider two contribution settings: a user can change arbitrarily many counts by at most one each, or can change only a small fixed number of counts by at most one. This makes the treatment cover both unrestricted and restricted sensitivity.

The paper also introduces a pay-what-you-get composition bound. An algorithm may return fewer than the requested k items, but privacy accounting decreases the available budget according to the number actually returned. This connects the privacy cost to the delivered output. Together, limited access requirements and output-sensitive accounting address practical obstacles to private selection over an unknown domain.
neurips-2019-practical-differentially-pr.tldr: Private top-k algorithms work without knowing the full item domain and account for privacy cost according to how many items they return.

paragraphs: Learning a high-dimensional data distribution involves both describing which observations are plausible and producing new samples that follow that description. This paper introduces a deep energy adversarial network, or DEAN, that assigns these roles to two generative networks. Their interaction is formulated using a goodness-of-fit test statistic.

One network learns an explicit energy-based distribution fitted to real data. The other is an implicit generator that produces samples. It is trained to reduce the goodness-of-fit statistic comparing its generated data with the energy-based distribution, encouraging its output distribution to approach the learned energy model. The test statistic therefore connects distribution learning with sample generation.

The authors train the two networks through a two-level alternating optimization procedure that also allows hyperparameters to be learned automatically. Experiments report high-quality generated samples compared with state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution is a coupled framework in which one model learns a target distribution and another learns to sample consistently with it, using statistical goodness of fit to define their relationship.
neurips-2019-two-generator-game-learning.tldr: DEAN couples an energy-based distribution learner with a sample generator through a goodness-of-fit objective and alternating optimization.
